featureMarkdown: Burn data disc from files / folders
featureHtml: Burn a data disc from files and folders
notesMarkdown: ISO 9660 + Joliet + UDF bridge; UDF 1.02 by default, 1.50 to 2.60 on request (`--udf-rev`). With the Windows writer (the default) on real discs on one drive (LG GP60NB50), every file read back identical: a DVD+RW, a DVD-R and a DVD+R (two sessions each on the DVD-R and DVD+R), and a dual-layer DVD+R holding 5.5 GB across both layers (Windows puts the layer break at half the data). A DVD-RW (Ritek) too, with one difference: Windows' writer formats a blank DVD-RW for overwriting before it writes, so it is never left open for more sessions (the burn says so when that was asked for); every file identical, also after writing it over past the part formatted first

featureMarkdown: Disc copy (one or two drives, multi-copy)
featureHtml: Copy a disc (one or two drives, several copies)
notesMarkdown: Swap prompts between copies; audio CDs copied track by track. A mixed-mode CD (data track first, then audio) is copied whole with direct drive commands turned on, otherwise only its audio; done once on a real drive (one drive, a CD-RW copied to a CD-R). An Enhanced CD (audio session, then a data session) is copied whole with direct drive commands on; that copy has run only in the built-in drive simulator. The source audio is read with error checks and re-reads, and a copy stops before writing when sectors still read wrong

The source audio is read with error checks and re-reads, and a copy stops before writing when sectors still read wrong; real-drive reports welcome
summaryHtml: Audio CDs are copied track by track, with swap prompts between copies. A mixed-mode CD has been copied whole once on a real drive; an Enhanced CD only in the drive simulator.

featureHtml: Rip an audio CD to WAV, FLAC, MP3, Opus or AAC + .cue
notesMarkdown: Reads the real TOC and CD-Text; optional MusicBrainz track names, release year and front cover (Cover Art Archive). When MusicBrainz lists editions that name tracks differently, the rip stops before reading the disc and asks which edition you have. Files can go straight into a library folder (`Artist\Album (Year)\NN - Title` by default, or your own naming template), in several formats from one rip, with `folder.jpg` and a `.cue` per album; MP3 can be constant bitrate or VBR (V0-V9). `convert-audio` (and the app's Convert Audio tab) converts files already on disk, keeping their tags and cover. AAC uses the encoder built into Windows; FLAC, MP3 and Opus use the optional ffmpeg download (no encoder is bundled). Ripping has run on a real drive (LG GP60NB50): tracks from CD-Rs and a CD-RW burned by IgnisDisc came back identical to the source audio. Gap detection (INDEX 00 marks in the `.cue`, hidden audio before track 1, pre-emphasis) has been tested on the virtual drive only, not on a real disc with such gaps. The encoders and output formats are otherwise tested on the virtual drive only; the built-in FLAC decoder (used for burning) is also checked against files made by the official flac 1.5.0 encoder

notesMarkdown: Detects your drive's offset from a disc in the AccurateRip database; optional opt-in CUETools Database (CTDB) track and disc CRC-32 lookup (`--verify-ctdb`, off by default) that also repairs a rip from CTDB parity and keeps the fix only when AccurateRip then matches. On a real CD the CTDB check matched the database and its repair data matched IgnisDisc's own calculation; the repair has fixed a real rip with damage added afterwards (zeroed sectors, flipped samples) against the live database, confirmed by AccurateRip, but has not yet met a physically scratched disc

notesMarkdown: Requires `ffmpeg.exe` (the 1-click download). Long movies are compressed to fit: before converting, the DVD-Video screen reads each movie's running time and says whether they fit a 4.7 GB DVD at full quality, compressed (with the video bitrate and how it will look), only on a dual-layer DVD, or on no DVD at all (Burn is then off). When a 4.7 GB DVD would have to compress and a dual-layer DVD would keep a clearly higher bitrate, it offers both (for example 3,587 kbps or full quality for a 2 h 20 min film), and a burn is refused before converting when the disc in the drive is too small. Each film becomes a title with a chapter every 5 minutes, English subtitles from an `.srt` beside it (or generated with the optional subtitle tool; the DVD-Video screen shows each movie's subtitle source with *Choose .srt...* and *No subtitles*), and a title menu with a still from each film and Play / Play with subtitles buttons. The navigation tables follow libdvdread's structures and were checked with libdvdnav (mpv, VLC). Played on one stand-alone player so far, an Xbox Series X: a film with menu, chapters and subtitles on a DVD+RW, and two films on a dual-layer DVD+R played across the layer change. Discs authored before 2026-11-14 did not play there. The authoring options (autoplay, action after a film, chapter interval, subtitles, video quality, title menu) have been checked in the test suite only; no disc made with a non-default choice has been burned or played yet

notesMarkdown: Optional 1-click download, nothing bundled: whisper.cpp 1.9.5 and its models, every file pinned by SHA-256 (`install-subtitle-tool`, or the button on the DVD-Video screen). On a PC with an NVIDIA GPU and driver 551.61 or newer it gets the CUDA build and the large-v3-turbo model (2.3 GB download). With an AMD or Intel GPU instead, integrated graphics included, it gets a Vulkan build of the same whisper.cpp source and the large-v3-turbo model (1.6 GB download): whisper.cpp publishes no Windows GPU build for these, so IgnisDisc's own GitHub workflow builds it, with a build provenance attestation. Any other PC gets the processor build and the smaller base model (160 MB). Measured on one PC, on an 86-minute animated feature with English dialogue, against its human-made subtitles: on an RTX 3090, 3.3 min from movie file to .srt (26 times real time) with a word error rate of 24.9%; processor build only (16-core desktop processor, base model), 3.4 min and 34.3%. Through the Vulkan build, speech recognition alone (from the extracted audio) took 18.1 min on Intel UHD Graphics 770 integrated graphics (26.0%), and 60 s on the RTX 3090 (26.1%; the CUDA build took 56 s on the same audio). The Vulkan build has not been run on an AMD GPU yet. The large model on that processor ran at 1.7 times real time (178 s for 5 minutes, about 50 minutes for this film), so the better model needs a GPU. The error rate counts wording the human subtitles shorten too; an invented place name was never heard right. The subtitles are machine-generated: check them before relying on them. `burn-dvd --generate-subtitles` ("Generate subtitles" on the DVD-Video screen) makes them for movies with no .srt beside them and puts them on the disc as its subtitle track. Authored end to end on the test PC from a 5-minute excerpt: the generated lines appear as the DVD subtitle track and on the menu's "Play with subtitles" button. A full-length film with generated subtitles was burned to a worn DVD+RW on one drive (LG GP60NB50, 2026-11-14), but the read-back check of that disc failed, so it is not counted as a good burn; no disc with generated subtitles has been played in a stand-alone player yet. Muxing the subtitle track needs a recent FFmpeg (the 1-click download): a 2021 build crashed on it

notesMarkdown: Audio CDs Session-at-Once and data/video discs without the Windows writer (`--native` on the command line, or "Direct drive commands" in the app — on by default in the app for audio CDs, falling back to the Windows writer if the drive does not offer Session-at-Once, for dual-layer DVD-Video, and for a DVD-RW, in the app and with burn-data and burn-iso, where a quick-erased disc that cannot be left open still goes to the Windows writer (a Settings switch, or --windows-writer on the command line, turns the DVD-RW default off); off by default elsewhere); the disc is always read back and compared. Run on real hardware on one drive so far (LG GP60NB50), on CD-R and CD-RW. Mixed-mode CDs (a Mode 1 data track, then audio) from a `.cue` file too: one CD-RW so far, where Windows read the data track's files back identical. A Mode 2 / CD-ROM XA data track (`MODE2/2352` or `MODE2/2336`) as track 1, and the write-offset correction on the audio part of a mixed-mode disc, have run only in the drive simulator, not on a real disc. Blank single-layer DVD-R, DVD-RW and DVD+R can also be written this way. A further session on a CD-R, CD-RW, DVD-R, DVD-RW or DVD+R left open is added the same way: on real discs on the same drive, three sessions each on a CD-RW, a CD-R and a DVD+R and four on a DVD-R, every file of every session identical (the first DVD-R try was refused with nothing written, because the drive rejects the writer's old track query on DVD; fixed before these runs); on a DVD-RW too, which must be fully erased before it can be left open: a second session added and the disc closed, every file of both sessions identical (Windows showed the new session after the disc was put back in). On real hardware so far two DVD-Rs on the same drive (Verbatim): one closed in one pass (372 MB), one left open, after which Windows' own writer added a second session; every file of each session identical when read through Windows. Two DVD+RWs too (Verbatim, 372 MB each, every file identical): a used one written over with leave to replace its data, and a new one, formatted first by the drive. A single-layer DVD+R too (Verbatim, 198 MB, finalized by the drive, every file identical). A DVD-RW too (Ritek): closed in one pass after a quick erase (63 MB; the drive took 6 minutes to close it), left open after a full erase (200 MB), and in overwrite mode written over past its formatted part, which the writer expanded first (230 MB); every file identical each time. A DVD-Video disc was written to a used DVD+RW this way too (a 60 s test card, 44 MB): every sector read back and the title decodes in full, this test card was not played in a stand-alone player (a later film disc was; see DVD-Video authoring). A dual-layer DVD+R too (Verbatim, the Ubuntu 26.04 image, 6.5 GB, with the layer break moved to where it was asked for; the drive reported it there and the disc's SHA-256 equalled the image). A two-film DVD-9 (103 and 86 minutes) went onto a dual-layer DVD+R the same way, with the layer break on the cell where the second film starts: every sector read back, the drive reported the break there, and an Xbox Series X played through the first film into the second across the layer change without a stop. Dual-layer DVD-R (layer jump recording, on drives that offer it), DVD-RAM, single-layer BD-R and BD-RE, leaving an audio CD open for a second data session (CD-Extra), that session's optional Blue Book layout (off by default: CD-ROM XA Mode 2 Form 1 with CDPLUS/INFO.CDP and PICTURES), and the optional Audio CD PAR2 recovery session (`--recovery-session` / `rip-audio --repair`) have run only in the built-in drive simulator, not on a real disc. Dual-layer DVD-R on a drive without layer jump recording, and multi-layer Blu-ray discs, still use the Windows writer

Dual-layer DVD-R (layer jump recording, on drives that offer it), DVD-RAM, single-layer BD-R and BD-RE, leaving an audio CD open for a second data session (CD-Extra), that session's optional Blue Book layout (off by default: CD-ROM XA Mode 2 Form 1 with CDPLUS/INFO.CDP and PICTURES), and the optional Audio CD PAR2 recovery session (--recovery-session / rip-audio --repair) have run only in the built-in drive simulator, not on a real disc. Dual-layer DVD-R on a drive without layer jump recording, and multi-layer Blu-ray discs, still use the Windows writer
summaryHtml: Writes without the Windows writer (--native; on by default in the app for audio CDs, dual-layer DVD-Video and DVD-RW), and always reads the disc back and compares it. Tested in one drive (LG GP60NB50) on CD-R, CD-RW, DVD-R, DVD-RW, DVD+R, DVD+RW and dual-layer DVD+R. DVD-RAM, dual-layer DVD-R, Blu-ray and CD-Extra have run only in the drive simulator.
